title: Evaluating AI
summary: Accuracy, precision and recall with a confusion matrix, benchmarks and their limits, hallucinations, and why models can be confidently wrong.

sections.heading: A worked example
paragraphs: Imagine testing a spam filter on 100 emails: 60 are really spam and 40 are real messages. The filter catches 45 of the 60 spam emails and misses 15. It also wrongly flags 5 real emails as spam and correctly leaves the other 35 alone. The table below, called a confusion matrix, organizes these four outcomes.

A true positive is spam correctly flagged (45). A false negative is spam that slipped through (15). A false positive is a real email wrongly flagged (5). A true negative is a real email correctly left alone (35).

sections.heading: Three key metrics
bullets: Accuracy: the share of all predictions that were correct. (45 + 35) / 100 = 80%.
Precision: of everything the model flagged as spam, how much really was spam? 45 / (45 + 5) = 90%.
Recall: of all the real spam, how much did the model catch? 45 / (45 + 15) = 75%.
paragraphs: Which metric matters most depends on the cost of each mistake. If false alarms are costly, such as blocking important school emails, focus on precision. If misses are costly, such as failing to flag a possible disease in a screening test, focus on recall. The F1 score combines precision and recall into one number.

sections.heading: When accuracy misleads
paragraphs: Suppose a disease affects 1 in 100 people. A lazy model that always says "healthy" is 99% accurate, yet it never finds a single sick person, so its recall is 0%. When one class is rare, accuracy alone can hide a useless model.

sections.heading: Benchmarks and their limits
paragraphs: A benchmark is a standard set of tasks used to measure and compare models. Benchmarks are useful, but a high score does not guarantee good real-world performance. Test questions can leak into training data (called data contamination), models can be tuned to a benchmark's quirks, and real users ask messier questions than any test.

sections.heading: Hallucinations
paragraphs: A hallucination is when an AI model states false or made-up information as if it were true, such as a fake quote, a wrong date or a citation to a paper that does not exist. Language models generate text that sounds likely, and their confident tone is not a sign that anything was checked. Gaps in training data and questions about events after the model's knowledge cutoff make errors more likely.
Protect yourself by checking important claims, especially names, numbers, quotes and sources, against reliable, independent sources. Asking the model "Are you sure?" is not a real check.

terms.definition: The share of all predictions a model got right.
terms.example: A model that is right on 80 of 100 test emails has 80% accuracy.

terms.definition: Of all the items a model labeled positive, the share that really were positive.
terms.example: If a filter flags 50 emails as spam and 45 really are spam, its precision is 90%.

terms.definition: Of all the items that really were positive, the share the model found.
terms.example: If there are 60 spam emails and the filter catches 45, its recall is 75%.

terms.definition: A table comparing a model's predictions with the actual answers, showing true and false positives and negatives.
terms.example: A 2-by-2 grid showing how many spam and real emails were sorted correctly and incorrectly.

terms.definition: A case the model correctly labeled as positive.
terms.example: A spam email that the filter correctly flags as spam.

terms.definition: A case the model wrongly labeled as positive (a false alarm).
terms.example: A real email from your teacher that gets sent to the spam folder.

terms.definition: A positive case the model missed by labeling it negative.
terms.example: A spam email that lands in your inbox.

terms.definition: A case the model correctly labeled as negative.
terms.example: A real email that the filter correctly leaves in your inbox.

terms.definition: A single metric that balances precision and recall (their harmonic mean).
terms.example: Two spam filters can be compared by their F1 scores when both precision and recall matter.

terms.definition: A standard set of tasks or questions used to measure and compare AI models.
terms.example: A collection of thousands of math problems used to compare how well different models reason.

terms.definition: When an AI model states false or made-up information as if it were true.
terms.example: A chatbot citing a research paper that does not exist.

terms.definition: When test questions or their answers appear in a model's training data, making its test score look better than it should.
terms.example: A model scores highly on a quiz because the quiz was posted online and ended up in its training data.

terms.definition: The point in time after which a model has little or no information from its training data.
terms.example: A model may not know about an election held after its knowledge cutoff.

questions.prompt: What does accuracy measure?
options: The share of all predictions that were correct
The share of predicted positives that were actually positive
The share of actual positives the model found
How fast the model runs
questions.answer: The share of all predictions that were correct
questions.explanation: Accuracy counts every correct prediction, positive or negative, out of the total. The second and third options describe precision and recall.

questions.prompt: Which metric answers the question "Of all the items the model flagged as positive, how many really were positive?"
options: precision
recall
accuracy
loss
questions.explanation: Precision looks only at what the model flagged and asks how much of it was right.

questions.prompt: Which metric answers the question "Of all the items that really were positive, how many did the model find?"
options: recall
precision
accuracy
loss
questions.explanation: Recall looks at all the real positives and asks how many the model caught.

questions.prompt: A spam filter is tested on 100 emails. It catches 45 of the 60 spam emails and wrongly flags 5 of the 40 real emails. What is its precision?
questions.explanation: Precision = true positives / everything flagged as spam = 45 / (45 + 5) = 90%.

questions.prompt: The same spam filter caught 45 of the 60 spam emails and wrongly flagged 5 of the 40 real emails. What is its recall?
questions.explanation: Recall = true positives / all real spam = 45 / 60 = 75%.

questions.prompt: The same spam filter caught 45 of the 60 spam emails and correctly left 35 of the 40 real emails alone. What is its accuracy?
questions.explanation: Accuracy = correct predictions / all predictions = (45 + 35) / 100 = 80%.

questions.prompt: Match each confusion matrix outcome to its meaning for a spam filter.

answer.definition: A real email wrongly flagged as spam
Spam that slipped through as a real email
A real email correctly left alone

questions.explanation: "True" or "false" says whether the model was right, and "positive" or "negative" says what it predicted.

questions.prompt: A rare disease affects 1 in 100 people. A model that always predicts "healthy" would have about what accuracy, and why is that misleading?
options: About 99%, but it never finds a single sick person, so its recall is 0%
About 1%, because it is always wrong
50%, because there are two possible answers
100%, because healthy people are the majority
questions.answer: About 99%, but it never finds a single sick person, so its recall is 0%
questions.explanation: It is right about the 99 healthy people but misses every sick one. With imbalanced data, accuracy alone can hide a useless model.

questions.prompt: A model can have high accuracy and still be useless if one class is very rare.
questions.explanation: Always predicting the common class can score high accuracy while never catching the rare cases that matter.

questions.prompt: For a disease screening tool, missing a real case is far worse than a false alarm that leads to a follow-up test. Which metric should the team prioritize?
options: Recall
Precision
Training speed
Number of parameters
questions.explanation: Recall measures how many real cases are caught. When misses are dangerous, high recall matters most.

questions.prompt: A school's email filter keeps blocking real messages from teachers as spam, and those false alarms are the bigger problem. Which metric should be improved?
options: Precision
Recall
Loss
Context window
questions.explanation: False positives lower precision. Improving precision means fewer real emails get wrongly flagged.

questions.prompt: What is an AI hallucination?
options: When a model produces information that sounds confident but is false or made up
When a model runs out of memory
When a model is turned off during training
When a model refuses to answer a question
questions.answer: When a model produces information that sounds confident but is false or made up
questions.explanation: Hallucinations are fluent, confident errors, such as invented quotes, facts or citations.

questions.prompt: What is the term for when an AI model states false or made-up information as if it were true?
options: hallucination
overfitting
precision
fine-tuning
questions.explanation: The term "hallucination" describes confident but false output. Checking important claims is the best defense.

questions.prompt: Why can language models be confidently wrong?
options: They generate text that sounds likely, and a confident tone does not mean the facts were checked
They are programmed to sound unsure only when they are right
They only make mistakes when the internet is down
They always know when they are wrong but hide it
questions.answer: They generate text that sounds likely, and a confident tone does not mean the facts were checked
questions.explanation: Fluency and correctness are different things. A model can write a polished, certain-sounding sentence that is false.

questions.prompt: What is a benchmark in AI?
options: A standard set of tasks or questions used to measure and compare models
A bench where engineers sit while training models
The final step of deploying a model
A type of neural network layer
questions.answer: A standard set of tasks or questions used to measure and compare models
questions.explanation: Benchmarks give everyone the same test so models can be compared fairly, although they have limits.

questions.prompt: A high score on a benchmark guarantees that a model will perform well in every real-world situation.
questions.explanation: Benchmarks cover only certain tasks and can be contaminated or gamed. Real-world use is messier than any test.

questions.prompt: What is data contamination when evaluating a model?
options: When test questions or their answers appeared in the model's training data, inflating its score
When a virus infects the training computer
When the model's output contains typos
When users send a model too many prompts
questions.answer: When test questions or their answers appeared in the model's training data, inflating its score
questions.explanation: If a model has already seen the test, its score measures memory rather than skill.

questions.prompt: What metric combines precision and recall into a single number?
options: F1 score
accuracy
loss
learning rate
questions.explanation: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is high only when both are high.

questions.prompt: A chatbot gives you a citation for a research paper, complete with authors and a title. What should you do before using it?
options: Search for the paper yourself to confirm it exists and says what the chatbot claims
Use it right away, since chatbots cannot invent citations
Ask the chatbot if it is sure, and trust a "yes"
Change the year so it looks more recent
questions.answer: Search for the paper yourself to confirm it exists and says what the chatbot claims
questions.explanation: Chatbots can produce realistic-looking citations to papers that do not exist. Always verify sources yourself.

questions.prompt: Asking a chatbot "Are you sure?" is a reliable way to confirm that a fact is true.
questions.explanation: The model may repeat or change its answer without checking anything. Reliable, independent sources are the real check.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for fact-checking an AI answer in order.
answer: Identify the specific claims, names, numbers and quotes
Look up each claim in reliable, independent sources
Compare what the sources say with the AI's answer
Correct or remove anything you could not confirm
questions.explanation: First find what needs checking, then check it, compare, and fix or drop unconfirmed claims.

questions.prompt: What is a confusion matrix?
options: A table that compares a model's predictions with the actual answers, showing each kind of correct and incorrect result
A list of words the model finds confusing
A chart of how long training took
A grid of GPU temperatures
questions.answer: A table that compares a model's predictions with the actual answers, showing each kind of correct and incorrect result
questions.explanation: The matrix shows true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives, which are used to calculate accuracy, precision and recall.

questions.prompt: For a spam filter, a real email that gets wrongly marked as spam is called a false ___ . Type the full term.
options: false positive
false negative
true positive
true negative
questions.explanation: The filter said "positive" (spam) and was wrong, so it is a false positive.

questions.prompt: Model A scores 85% on a benchmark and Model B scores 84%. Later, researchers find that some of the test questions were in Model A's training data. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Model A's score may be inflated, so the comparison is not reliable
Model A is definitely the better model
Model B must have cheated
Benchmarks can never be used for anything
questions.answer: Model A's score may be inflated, so the comparison is not reliable
questions.explanation: Contamination means Model A may have memorized some answers. A one-point gap tells us little in that situation.

questions.prompt: What is a model's knowledge cutoff?
options: The point in time after which it has little or no information from its training data
The maximum length of a prompt
The moment the model is deleted
The number of facts the model can store
questions.answer: The point in time after which it has little or no information from its training data
questions.explanation: Models are trained on data collected up to some date. Questions about later events are more likely to get wrong or outdated answers.

questions.prompt: A model can do well on its test set but worse after launch if real-world data is different from the data it was tested on.
questions.explanation: Test results only predict performance on data similar to the test set. If users or conditions differ, performance can drop.

questions.prompt: Match each metric to the question it answers.

answer.definition: What fraction of all predictions were right?
When it says "yes," how often is it right?
Of all the real "yes" cases, how many did it catch?
What single number balances precision and recall?

questions.explanation: Each metric looks at a different slice of the confusion matrix, so they can tell different stories about the same model.
